problems.description: Measured convention score 0.74 (14 violations) is dominated by pre-existing PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE issues in celery_config.py, db.py, __init__.py, and app.py — files this commit did not author. The commit's own delta (test_app.py) is convention-clean snake_case; the score overstates this session's non-adherence.
Test fixture relies on importlib.reload(app_module) to re-read the monkeypatched DATABASE env var, revealing an env-read-at-import coupling in app.py's DB config that makes it awkward to test.

test_list_tasks_ordered_desc depends on created_at discriminating between three rapid inserts; if created_at has whole-second granularity the ORDER BY DESC tie is undefined and the assertion could be flaky.

strengths: Complete CRUD test coverage including error paths (400 missing/blank title, 404 not-found) across create, list, get, and update
The behavior change (ORDER BY created_at DESC) is explicitly pinned by a dedicated test, so the edit is verified rather than asserted
Isolated test DB via tempfile + monkeypatched DATABASE env with proper cleanup (os.close/os.unlink); zero new bugs, smells, or duplications per SonarQube delta
commit_reviews.summary: Clean greenfield session that adds a full, isolated pytest suite and pins a sensible newest-first ordering change with an explicit test — the only caveat is that the measured 0.74 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched.

problems.description: SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded well-known value ('dev-secret-change-me-in-production-32b') when the env var is unset; any deployed instance missing DATABASE-style env parity gets forgeable JWTs. Should fail fast (raise) instead of silently using a public key.

_migrate_add_owner_id only adds the column; pre-existing task rows get NULL owner_id and become permanently invisible to all users (get_tasks filters on owner_id). No backfill/reassignment policy for legacy data.
The diff adds +0 new files and touches no tests, yet introduces two new auth endpoints, a decorator, and per-owner query scoping — all of which are regression-prone paths with no coverage.
Password has no length/complexity floor at registration, and tokens carry no iat/nbf; a deleted user's token remains valid until 24h expiry since login_required never re-checks user existence.

strengths: Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never stored in plaintext; JWT carries an expiry with timezone-aware timestamps.
Per-user ownership (owner_id) enforced consistently across every task route, closing an IDOR hole the baseline had.
login_required decorator is idiomatic: functools.wraps preserves metadata and Flask `g` carries user_id cleanly.
Adds a migration helper for pre-existing databases — a thoughtful touch for a multi-session story baseline.
Respects the existing single-file structure and conventions: same section-separator comments, snake_case functions, parameterized queries, proper HTTP status codes (400/401/409/201).
SonarQube reports zero new bugs, smells, or duplications.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent Session-2 feature that layers JWT auth and per-user task scoping onto the existing single-file Flask baseline with sound security primitives and pattern-following structure, at the cost of a hardcoded fallback secret and orphaned pre-existing task rows.

problems.description: celery_config.py declares module-level Celery settings in snake_case (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes, ...); the repo's static convention check expects UPPER_CASE module constants, and this is the diff's only net-new naming violation.

_notify_task_completed swallows a broad `except Exception` around .delay(); the resilience guarantee is good but a targeted catch (ConnectionError/OperationalError) would avoid masking real config errors — the broker-failure test only exercises ConnectionError.
Duplications +3.2%: the FakeCeleryTask and BrokenTask stubs duplicate delay-capture logic and could be collapsed into the shared fixture.

The 0.74 convention score is partly inflated by violations in files untouched by this diff (db.py, __init__.py, and a pre-existing app.py class flag); this commit's own introduced violations are confined to celery_config.py naming.

strengths: Notification fires only on a status transition to completed (no re-notification), verified by a dedicated test.
Broker-failure resilience: the try/except guard keeps the request path alive even when the broker is unreachable, and that behavior is explicitly tested.
Thorough test coverage: transition, non-transition, title-only, cross-user 404, re-notify suppression, broker failure, and task registration.
Clean separation of concerns: celery_config.py (config) / tasks.py (task definition) / app.py (integration) with env-var-overridable broker URLs.
Fire-and-forget async dispatch keeps request latency low; type hints on the new public functions; mock-email derivation is documented as a schema workaround.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, cleanly separated async notification integration that respects existing app patterns and isolates broker failures, though it introduces lowercase Celery config constants against repo convention and carries a modest debt load (smells +2, complexity +6, duplications +3.2%).

problems.description: BaseRepository.update and UserRepository.update build UPDATE SQL via f-string column-name interpolation from **fields (repositories/base.py, user_repository.py). Only internal callers feed it, but the generic contract invites caller-controlled column names; an allowlist or per-column setter would be safer.

Measured convention score 0.74 with 14 violations. Several listed on new/modified files appear to be analyzer false positives: db.py and app.py contain no classes yet are flagged 'Classes should use PascalCase', and repositories/__init__.py flags 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' for the dunder __all__.

celery_config.py (pre-existing from Session 3, present in this tree) still carries 3 violations — lowercase Celery settings are standard for that framework, so this is a measurement of convention rather than a defect introduced here.
BaseRepository.table_name is annotated `str = None` — annotation and default disagree; harmless but sloppy typing for an ABC.

strengths: Centralizes ALL SQLite access behind db.py (connection + schema) and the repositories/ CRUD layer, removing raw SQL from route handlers entirely.
Preserves security semantics in the move: task rows stay owner-scoped and non-owned/missing tasks still 404, so existence is never leaked.
Introduces an app factory (create_app) with request-scoped g.db and teardown_appcontext(close_db), materially improving testability over the module-level globals.
Migrations are additive and idempotent (owner_id, then email), and run on startup against pre-existing databases — no data loss or destructive DDL.
Repository instances receive get_db via constructor injection, keeping them cheap to create and safe to reuse across requests.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive refactor that cleanly extracts a repository layer and app factory (fitting the seed's 'good seams' intent) while preserving auth/scoping contracts; the measured 0.74 convention score is dragged down partly by analyzer false positives on class-less modules and Celery's standard lowercase settings, so qualitative convention quality is slightly better than the number suggests.

problems.description: Sort key silently changed from created_at DESC to id DESC in get_page. The existing test_list_tasks_ordered_desc only passes because insertion order coincides with id order; the behavioral change is undocumented and would break if created_at is ever set explicitly.
GET /tasks response shape changed from a bare list to an envelope {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking API contract change with no version bump or compatibility shim for existing clients.

Rate limiting adds a Redis storage dependency (default redis://localhost:6379/1). With swallow_errors=True the limiter fails open silently when Redis is unavailable, disabling a security control without notice; a fail-closed mode or documented tradeoff would be safer for an auth-adjacent feature.
SELECT COUNT(*) total runs on every page request; acceptable at task-manager scale but unbounded as the table grows.

Measured convention score 0.74 is dominated by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, db.py, __init__.py); this commit's own code (rate_limit_key, get_page, DEFAULT_PAGE_LIMIT/MAX_PAGE_LIMIT, Limiter) adheres to snake_case/UPPER_CASE/PascalCase.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination keyed on stable id with the limit+1 lookahead pattern for next_cursor — no offset drift, consistent ordering
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user (bearer token) with IP fallback and a single shared bucket via application_limits, with a thorough rationale in the docstring
Pagination lives in the repository layer (get_page), keeping the route handler thin and respecting the existing data-access pattern

Solid test coverage: response-shape updates, dedicated pagination tests, limiter.reset() in the fixture, and direct DB seeding (_seed_tasks_directly) to avoid exhausting the rate-limit budget under test
Input validation for cursor/limit with clamping to MAX_PAGE_LIMIT and a JSON 429 handler consistent with the API error envelope
commit_reviews.summary: High-quality cross-cutting commit (cursor pagination + per-user rate limiting) that follows existing patterns and ships with thorough tests, but it silently changes list ordering to id DESC, breaks the GET /tasks response contract with an envelope, and adds a Redis-backed limiter that fails open — while the measured 0.74 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 2 retrofitted authentication (users table + owner_id) onto an already-populated tasks schema, requiring a runtime migration (_migrate_add_owner_id); pre-existing tasks are left with NULL owner_id, effectively orphaned to any authenticated user
The Session 2 schema decision to give users no email field permanently constrained Session 3's notification feature, which had to derive mock addresses (_mock_email_for) instead of sending real email
Session 5 silently switched the task ordering key from created_at to id for cursor pagination, a behavior change layered on top of the Session 1 regression test's ordering contract
SECRET_KEY and rate-limit storage default to hardcoded dev values (dev-secret-change-me-in-production-32b, redis://localhost:6379/1) that persisted through all five sessions without hardening
key_decisions: Session 1 caught and reverted the injected bug (reversed ORDER BY) immediately, locking intended behavior with a dedicated regression test (test_list_tasks_ordered_desc)
JWT-based auth with password hashing and an owner-scoped data model added via schema migration rather than a clean re-seed
Fire-and-forget Celery notification task on task completion, wrapped in try/except so a broker hiccup never breaks the request
Repository pattern extraction in Session 4 (ABC BaseRepository + TaskRepository/UserRepository) as a behavior-preserving refactor — test count stayed flat at 34
Session 5 production hardening: cursor-based keyset pagination (id DESC, limit+1 lookahead) and flask-limiter rate limiting keyed per-authenticated-user with a single shared bucket
Separated db.py connection/schema management with env-var DATABASE read per connection to keep tests isolated
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across all five sessions. The story opened with Session 1 fixing the injected seed bug and establishing a 11-test baseline, then layered on JWT auth with a schema migration (Session 2), an async Celery notification integration with graceful degradation (Session 3), a clean repository-layer refactor that preserved behavior exactly — test count unchanged at 34 (Session 4) — and closed with production-grade cross-cutting concerns: cursor pagination and per-user rate limiting (Session 5). The codebase grew from a single 130-line file into a layered architecture (db, repositories/, celery tasks, auth, rate limiting) while the test suite expanded from 11 to 47 passing tests (117 → 651 test lines), with every session's test_executed_success true and the final suite green.
story_review.summary: A textbook monotonic progression from greenfield to production-ready — bug fix, feature, integration, refactor, and cross-cutting hardening with steadily growing, all-green test coverage — marred only by minor schema-driven constraints (mock emails, owner-less legacy rows) inherited from early auth decisions.
